summary: Adds MD5-based authentication to RIP version 2, improving on the unauthenticated or plain-password service. It was replaced by RFC 4822.

eli5.summary: Routers show a secret stamp to prove that updates are real and have not been faked.

questions: how does rip-2 verify routing updates
subtitle: Adds cryptographic authentication to RIP routing updates.

tldr.problem: RIP version 2 routing announcements could be forged or intercepted, as the original protocol offered no real authentication. Simple passwords transmitted in the clear were vulnerable to passive attacks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds MD5-based authentication to RIP-2 messages, where the sender appends a keyed digest of the message. The receiver verifies the digest using the same key and rejects any message whose digest does not match.
tldr.outcome: Routers can now authenticate routing updates and detect forged messages. The approach uses a non-decreasing sequence number to prevent replays. RFC 4822 later supersedes this with improved specifications.

today: RFC 2082 is a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 4822, which provides a more robust and updated specification for RIP-2 authentication. RFC 4822 is the current recommended approach for securing RIP-2 messages.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RIP-2 is a distance-vector routing protocol that allows routers to share which networks they can reach. The original protocol offered either no authentication or only plain-text passwords, which are vulnerable to passive attacks where an attacker captures the password from the network and reuses it.

This RFC introduces MD5 authentication for RIP-2, a cryptographic mechanism that protects against forgery and message modification. The sender computes a one-way hash of the message using a secret key, and the receiver verifies this hash. Since the key is never transmitted in the clear, an attacker cannot easily forge valid messages.

The approach also includes a sequence number to defend against replay attacks, where an old captured message is replayed to disrupt routing. While sequence numbers alone cannot prevent all replays, they make long-term replay attacks much harder.
sections.eli5: Routing updates now come with a secret stamp that proves they are real. An attacker cannot make up a fake stamp without knowing the secret.

sections.title: Message Format and Header Structure
sections.content:
The RIP-2 message structure is modified to carry the authentication data. A standard RIP-2 message has an 8-byte header and an array of 20-byte route records. When MD5 authentication is used, the message header includes a new authentication type field set to 3, and the field that normally holds a simple password is reused to hold metadata about the digest.

The RIP-2 packet format includes four metadata fields in the authentication trailer: an authentication type (3 for MD5), a 16-bit offset pointing to where the digest begins in the message, an 8-bit key identifier to select which key was used, and an 8-bit authentication data length. A 32-bit sequence number completes the trailer, followed by the actual MD5 digest (16 bytes).

When computing the MD5 hash, the RIP-2 key (16 bytes) is appended to the message, padding and length fields are added according to RFC 1321, and the hash is calculated. The digest overwrites the RIP-2 key in the transmitted message, keeping the packet self-contained.
sections.eli5: The routing message gets extra fields that describe which secret key was used and a stamp at the end made from that key.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Messages
sections.content:
When a router sends an authenticated RIP-2 message, it selects a valid key from those configured on the outgoing interface. Each key has a key identifier, which the sender includes in the message so the receiver knows which key to use. The sender computes the MD5 digest over the entire message plus the secret key, pads and length fields as defined by RFC 1321, and appends the digest to the message.

On reception, the receiver extracts the key identifier and interface, looks up the corresponding secret key, and recomputes the MD5 digest using the same algorithm. If the computed digest does not match the received digest, the message is discarded immediately. If the receiver has recently heard from this neighbor and the sequence number in the message is less than the last sequence number received, the message is also discarded to prevent replay attacks.

If a router reboots and loses its sequence number state but remembers the key and key identifier, it MUST send its first packet with sequence number zero. This opens a small replay-attack window, which is why implementers are urged to store sequence numbers in stable storage.
sections.eli5: To send, pick a secret, stamp the message with it. To receive, look up the same secret and check the stamp. If the stamp doesn't match or is old, throw away the message.

sections.title: Key Management and Rollover
sections.content:
Authentication keys must be changed regularly to limit the damage from key compromise. This RFC requires implementations to store multiple keys on an interface at once, each with a key identifier, a lifetime (start and end time), and an algorithm identifier. Manual key distribution is required, allowing an administrator to specify keys and their lifetimes on the router console or via management interface.

To achieve a smooth rollover, the new key must be configured on all routers before the old key expires. The new key's lifetime should begin a few minutes before the old key expires, allowing both keys to be valid for an overlap period. During this overlap, senders may use either key, and receivers will accept either. The key identifier in each message tells the receiver which key to use for verification.

Two pathological cases require special handling: during key switchover, some routers may not yet have the new key, so a router SHOULD detect which keys its neighbors are using and may transmit with both old and new keys. If the last key on an interface expires, the router SHOULD treat it as having infinite lifetime rather than reverting to unauthenticated messages, and should notify the network manager.
sections.eli5: Like changing locks on doors: the new key is installed before the old one stops working, so there is time for everyone to switch. If someone forgets, the door stays locked rather than becoming unlocked.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limitations
sections.content:
This mechanism protects against passive and active attacks on RIP-2 messages, providing authentication and integrity. However, it does NOT provide confidentiality: the routing information inside the message remains in clear text. An attacker can still see which networks are being advertised, which routes are being taken, and the topology.

The security depends entirely on the strength of the MD5 algorithm (which should be considered cryptographically weak by modern standards), the quality of the key, and the correct implementation of the mechanism in all participating routers. Compromise of SNMP security (if SNMP is used to manage RIP-2 keys) could also compromise RIP-2. Changing keys via unencrypted SNMP is as risky as sending passwords in the clear.

Protection against traffic analysis is also not provided: an attacker can still count and analyze the flow of routing messages even if they cannot forge them. Bulk link encryption could be used to protect against traffic analysis if needed.
sections.eli5: The stamp proves the message is real, but it does not hide what the message says. Good keys and correct code matter; a weak key or implementation mistake breaks everything.
